1. The animation shows the typical gap between 30-year and 15-year mortgage rates, using Freddie Mac weekly survey data. The gap is shown by decade. A small figure named Tessa, standing by a house, is labeled "illustrative". The frames are marked "US only, history, not a forecast."

2. Bars rise and highlight one decade at a time. The labels fill in as they go. The 1991 to 1999 bar reads $15,118 and 0.46 point. The 2000s bar reads $14,210 and 0.45 point. The 2010s bar reads $20,374 and 0.72 point. A last bar, with no decade label, reads 0.70 point. The dollar figures appear from the start and the rate gaps are added later. A faint rate line runs behind the bars.

3. In this data, the 30-year rate has typically been about half a point to three-quarters of a point higher than the 15-year rate. The gap was about 0.45 to 0.46 point in the 1990s and 2000s. It was about 0.70 to 0.72 point in the 2010s and the latest period. The frames don't say what the dollar amounts measure. They might be interest or payment differences, but that is a guess.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer would only learn that a 15-year loan has usually carried a somewhat lower rate than a 30-year loan. Nothing in it says whether to pay extra on a mortgage or invest the spare cash.

5. The animation did not suggest any advice. Because the only on-screen message is "history, not a forecast," any pay-down-or-invest conclusion would be my own, and I am not drawing one from these frames.
